short: The human effort to work out Islamic law from its sources, and the rulings that result.
long: The word means understanding. Fiqh is not the same as shari'ah: shari'ah is the guidance God revealed, fiqh is what scholars understood of it, which is why qualified people reach different answers. Books of fiqh nearly all run in the same order: purification and prayer first, then fasting, zakat and hajj, then marriage, trade, inheritance and the courts.

short: The science of how rulings are derived: which sources count, and how they are read.
long: Literally the roots of fiqh. Where fiqh gives you the answer, usul al-fiqh gives you the method: the four sources agreed by the Sunni schools are the Qur'an, the Sunnah, ijma' and qiyas, together with rules for language, abrogation and conflicting evidence. Al-Shafi'i's Risalah is the earliest surviving book devoted to the subject.

short: The whole of what God revealed as guidance: belief, worship, character and law together.
long: The word literally means the path to water, and the Qur'an uses it for the way God set out for the Prophet to follow. It is far wider than law in the modern sense; most of it concerns prayer, fasting, honesty and family, and only a small portion concerns courts and punishment. Shari'ah is the revelation itself, while fiqh is the scholarly understanding of it, and collapsing the two makes human opinion sound divine.

short: The disciplined effort of a qualified scholar to derive a ruling from the sources.
long: The root means to exert oneself to the limit. It applies where the texts are not decisive, since nobody performs ijtihad against a clear and settled ruling. Classical scholars set demanding conditions for the mujtahid, including Arabic, command of the Qur'an and hadith, and knowledge of where consensus lies. The Prophet taught that one who judges by ijtihad and is right has two rewards, and one who tries sincerely and is wrong still has one.

short: Following a qualified scholar's ruling without knowing the underlying evidence yourself.
long: It is what most Muslims do most of the time, and the Qur'an tells those who do not know to ask those who do. Scholars differ over its limits: some hold a layperson should commit to one school for coherence, others allow asking any trustworthy scholar, and all agree taqlid is not followed against a clear text one actually knows. The word is also used critically, for copying without thought, which is a different matter from consulting an expert.

short: A school of law: a settled method of deriving rulings, carried by generations of scholars.
long: The plural is madhahib, and the word means a way gone along. Four Sunni schools survive with a living scholarly tradition: Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali. They agree on the pillars and on the great majority of rulings, and differ mostly in method and in detail. A madhhab is not a sect, and a Hanafi and a Shafi'i pray behind one another without difficulty.

short: The school of Abu Hanifah, the most widely followed, known for careful reasoning and analogy.
long: Named for Abu Hanifah al-Nu'man ibn Thabit of Kufa, who died in 150 AH, and set down by his students Abu Yusuf and al-Shaybani. It is the school of most Muslims in Turkey, the Balkans, Central Asia, South Asia and much of the Levant and Egypt. Its distinctive features include a strong use of istihsan and of local custom, and a separate ruling category of wajib standing just below fard.

short: The school of Malik ibn Anas of Madinah, weighted towards the practice of that city.
long: Malik died in 179 AH, and his Muwatta is among the earliest surviving books of hadith and law together. The school prevails across North and West Africa and parts of the Gulf. It gives particular weight to 'amal ahl al-Madinah, the living practice of the people of Madinah, on the reasoning that a whole city's inherited habit is itself evidence, and it makes heavy use of maslahah and of blocking the means.

short: The school of al-Shafi'i, known for tight textual method and a systematic theory of sources.
long: Muhammad ibn Idris al-Shafi'i died in 204 AH and wrote the Risalah, the first surviving work of usul al-fiqh. His school prevails in Egypt, East Africa, Yemen, Kurdistan and much of Southeast Asia. It leans on hadith more readily than the Hanafis do, and it rejects istihsan as a source in its own right, holding that preference without evidence is lawmaking.

short: The school of Ahmad ibn Hanbal, the most text bound of the four, strongest in Arabia.
long: Ahmad ibn Hanbal died in 241 AH and is remembered as much for his endurance under persecution as for his law. In worship the school stays close to the reports and is cautious about opinion. In transactions it is unusually permissive, holding that any contract is valid unless something forbids it. Ibn Taymiyyah and Ibn al-Qayyim wrote from within this school.

short: The agreement of the qualified scholars of one generation on a single ruling.
long: It is the third of the four agreed sources, after the Qur'an and the Sunnah. Certain ijma' is rare, and mostly concerns matters everyone already knows, such as the five daily prayers and the prohibition of wine. Scholars differ over whether a consensus after the Companions can ever be verified across a scattered world, so a claim of ijma' is something to check rather than accept on sight.

short: Analogy: extending a known ruling to a new case that shares the same underlying reason.
long: The classic example is extending the prohibition of wine to every intoxicant, because the reason behind the ruling is intoxication rather than grapes. It has four parts: the original case, the new case, the ruling, and the 'illah or effective cause, and identifying the 'illah is the difficult part. All four Sunni schools accept qiyas as a source; the Zahiri school rejected it and worked from the texts alone.

short: Local custom, which fiqh accepts as a decider where revelation has left a matter open.
long: If a contract says a reasonable quantity, or a delivery in good time, it is 'urf that decides what those words mean. It cannot make lawful what the texts forbid; it fills gaps and defines undefined terms. Because customs change, rulings resting on 'urf change with them, which is why the same school can give different answers in different centuries or countries without contradicting itself.

short: Public benefit, weighed as a legal consideration where no specific text settles the matter.
long: Its full name is al-maslahah al-mursalah, the untethered benefit, meaning one that revelation neither commands nor forbids by name. Registering marriages, compiling the Qur'an into one volume and building prisons were all defended this way. The schools differ over how far it may reach: Malikis and Hanbalis use it most freely, Shafi'is more narrowly, and all of them insist it can never overturn a clear text.

short: Necessity: the state in which something forbidden becomes permitted in order to preserve life.
long: The Qur'an allows a starving person to eat forbidden meat without sin, provided he is not seeking to transgress. Jurists built a maxim on it, that necessity makes the forbidden permitted, and bounded it with a second, that necessity is measured strictly by its extent. Hardship and inconvenience are not darurah; the classical threshold is real danger to life, limb, mind, lineage or property.

short: A concession: permission to do the easier thing when a recognised excuse applies.
long: Shortening prayer while travelling, breaking the fast when ill, and wiping over socks are all rukhsah. The Qur'an states plainly that God intends ease for you and does not intend hardship, and the Prophet is reported to have said God loves His concessions to be taken as He loves His commands to be obeyed. Taking a concession you genuinely qualify for is not weakness, and refusing one out of scruple is not extra piety.

short: The original ruling, before any concession applies: the default rather than the exception.
long: 'Azimah and rukhsah are a matched pair. Praying four rak'ahs is the 'azimah; shortening them on a journey is the rukhsah. Scholars differ over which is better for someone who qualifies for a concession, though most hold that where the Prophet clearly took the concession himself, as with breaking the fast on a hard journey, taking it is preferred.

short: Permitted. Anything revelation has not forbidden, which is the great majority of things.
long: The word means loosed or untied. In ordinary worldly matters the default is permission, so the burden of proof lies on whoever claims a thing is forbidden, not on the person doing it. In food it usually means meat slaughtered properly and free of pork, blood and intoxicants. But halal covers earnings, speech and work at least as much as it covers dinner.

short: Forbidden. Leaving it is rewarded, and doing it deliberately is a sin.
long: The list is far shorter than people assume: shirk, killing, theft, interest, intoxicants, pork, gambling, zina, and injustice to others. Something is haram only on clear evidence, and calling a disputed matter haram is itself a serious step, since the Qur'an warns against declaring things lawful and unlawful without knowledge. The same root also means sacred and inviolable, which is why the mosque in Makkah is al-Masjid al-Haram.

short: Disliked but not forbidden: leaving it is rewarded, doing it brings no sin.
long: Wasting water in wudu, and eating raw garlic before going to the mosque, are standard examples. Hanafis split the category in two: makruh tahriman, close to forbidden and sinful to do, and makruh tanzihan, merely unbecoming. The other three schools work with a single category. So a Hanafi and a Shafi'i can use the same word and mean noticeably different things, which is worth checking before you take offence or comfort.

short: Recommended: rewarded if done, with no blame for leaving it.
long: It covers the great mass of good practice, from the voluntary prayers around the obligatory ones to greeting people first and using the siwak. Mustahabb, mandub, sunnah and nafl are used almost interchangeably, with fine distinctions between the schools. Nobody is called to account for missing a mustahabb, which is why it should never be pressed on another person as though it were fard.

short: The technical term in legal theory for a recommended act: the same idea as mustahabb.
long: Literally, something invited or called to. Legal theorists prefer mandub, while practical books of fiqh usually say mustahabb or simply sunnah. Hanafis grade the recommended further, into sunnah mu'akkadah, which the Prophet kept up consistently, and mustahabb or nafl, which he did from time to time. On that grading, habitually dropping a sunnah mu'akkadah is blameworthy, though it is not sin in the way abandoning a fard is.

short: Neutral: neither rewarded nor blamed, permitted and left entirely to your choice.
long: Which colour you wear and what you eat for breakfast are mubah, and most of ordinary life sits inside this category. A mubah act can become worship through intention, since eating so as to have strength to pray is rewarded, and sleeping so as to rise for fajr is rewarded. This is where the maxim that matters are judged by their intentions does its quietest and most useful work.

short: Obligatory: required by decisive evidence, and sinful to abandon without an excuse.
long: The five daily prayers, the fast of Ramadan and zakat are fard. Hanafis reserve the word for what is proved beyond doubt and use wajib for what rests on a single strong report, so for them denying a fard is disbelief while denying a wajib is not. The other three schools treat fard and wajib as two names for one thing, which explains a good deal of apparent disagreement in books.

short: Obligatory. In the Hanafi school, a step below fard, resting on slightly weaker evidence.
long: For Malikis, Shafi'is and Hanbalis, wajib and fard are two words for one category. Hanafis separate them: the witr prayer and the sacrifice at Eid al-Adha are wajib rather than fard, so neglecting them is sinful while denying them is not disbelief. In hajj the distinction has a practical edge, since a missed wajib can be repaired by a sacrifice while a missed pillar cannot.

short: An individual obligation: every responsible Muslim must perform it personally.
long: Prayer, fasting Ramadan, zakat when you own the nisab, and hajj once if you are able. Nobody can discharge these on your behalf, and another person doing them does not lift them from you. Learning enough to practise your own religion is also fard 'ayn, which is why the basics of purification, prayer and honest earning are everybody's business and not only the scholars'.

short: A communal obligation: if enough people carry it out, it is lifted from everyone else.
long: The funeral prayer, memorising the Qur'an, medicine, and returning a greeting given to a group all fall here. If nobody does it, everyone capable shares the blame; once it is covered, it becomes merely recommended for the rest. Much of what a community actually needs, from judges and doctors to those who wash the dead, is organised under this single heading.

short: Intention, which decides what an act legally is, not merely whether it is rewarded.
long: The Prophet said that actions are only by their intentions, and jurists turned this into the first of the great legal maxims: matters are judged by their objectives. It settles whether a wash is a bath or a wudu, whether money handed over is a gift, a loan or a repayment, and whether ambiguous words of divorce take effect. In worship the intention lives in the heart; in contracts what you say and do binds you as well, because other people have relied on it.

short: The Islamic marriage contract, formed by offer, acceptance, witnesses and a mahr.
long: The word means to join. Marriage in Islam is a contract rather than a sacrament, and consent is its foundation: the Prophet annulled a marriage a woman told him she had not agreed to. Requirements differ a little between schools: the majority require a wali to contract on the bride's behalf, while Hanafis allow an adult woman to contract her own. Marriage is strongly encouraged rather than obligatory, and celibacy as a religious discipline has no place in Islam.

short: The gift of money or property the groom owes the bride, which belongs to her alone.
long: The Qur'an tells men to give it graciously, as a free gift. It is not a bride price paid to her family, and nobody else has any claim on it. It may be paid at once or deferred, and there is no fixed amount: the Prophet told one man to look for even an iron ring, and in the end married him to her for the Qur'an he had memorised, while extravagance was discouraged. If a marriage ends before consummation, half is normally due.

short: The wedding feast held after the marriage, and a strongly confirmed sunnah on the groom.
long: The Prophet told 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf to hold one even if only with a single sheep, and he taught that answering the invitation is a duty on those invited unless they have an excuse. Most scholars hold the walimah itself is a confirmed sunnah rather than obligatory. He also warned against a feast to which only the rich are invited and the poor are turned away, which is the part most often forgotten.

short: Divorce pronounced by the husband, which Islamic law permits but treats as a last resort.
long: The Qur'an gives it a whole surah and sets out a careful procedure: a single pronouncement, then a waiting period during which the couple may simply resume, with two further chances before the separation becomes final. Three pronouncements in one sitting are counted as three by the majority and as one by a minority, and this is among the oldest live disputes in fiqh. A woman who wishes to end a marriage uses khul' or asks a judge for faskh instead.

short: The waiting period a woman observes after divorce or a husband's death before remarrying.
long: After divorce it is three quru', which Hanafis and Hanbalis read as menstrual cycles and Malikis and Shafi'is as the purities between them, or three months for a woman who does not menstruate; after a husband's death, four months and ten days; and if she is pregnant, until she gives birth. Its purposes are to show there is no pregnancy, to leave room for reconciliation, and to mark the ending. In a revocable divorce she keeps housing and maintenance, and the husband may take her back without a new contract.

short: Divorce sought by the wife, usually by returning the mahr in exchange for her release.
long: Its basis is the Qur'anic statement that there is no blame on either of them in what she gives to be free, and the case of the wife of Thabit ibn Qays, who returned the garden he had given her. Scholars differ over whether the husband must agree or a judge may impose it, and over whether khul' counts as an irrevocable divorce or as an annulment, which changes the waiting period that follows. She does not need to prove wrongdoing to ask for it.

short: A relative you may never marry, and before whom the rules of covering are relaxed.
long: The Qur'an lists them: parents, children, siblings, aunts and uncles, nieces and nephews, along with relations formed by marriage such as a mother in law, and milk relations formed by nursing in infancy. The familiar phrase about travelling with a mahram refers to this same category, together with the husband. A cousin is not a mahram, which surprises many people, and neither is a brother in law.

short: The part of the body that must be covered, which varies by person and by setting.
long: For a man all four schools say from the navel to the knee. For a woman before unrelated men the schools differ: the majority cover everything except the face and hands, some Hanbalis and later Shafi'is include the face, and Hanafis also exempt the feet. Among other women and before mahrams the requirement is much lighter, and in prayer it differs again. It is a rule about dignity in company, not a claim that the body is shameful.

short: The covering a Muslim woman wears in public, most often a headscarf with modest clothing.
long: The command to draw the khimar over the neckline stands in Surah al-Nur, directly after the command to believing men to lower their gaze; the outer garment, the jilbab, is in Surah al-Ahzab. The word itself means a screen or curtain, and in the Qur'an it usually means a barrier rather than a garment; the everyday sense of headscarf is later usage. The schools agree on covering the hair and body and differ over the face and hands.

short: Interest or unjust increase on a loan or exchange, forbidden in the Qur'an in severe terms.
long: Two forms are named: riba al-fadl, an unequal swap of the same commodity hand to hand, and riba al-nasi'ah, the increase charged for time, which is what an interest bearing loan involves. The Qur'an permits trade and forbids riba in the same breath, and the objection is to money multiplying from money with no shared risk and no real goods. Scholars differ sharply over how far the ruling extends into modern banking, and Islamic finance is the attempt to answer that.

short: Excessive uncertainty in a contract, which makes the deal invalid.
long: The Prophet forbade the gharar sale, and the stock examples jurists give are the young of an animal not yet born, and the fish still in the water. The problem is not risk, which every honest trade carries, but not knowing what you are buying, at what price, or whether it exists at all. Minor uncertainty is tolerated, since no contract is perfectly precise. Scholars invoke gharar when questioning conventional insurance and some derivative contracts, and takaful was designed as an answer to it.

short: A contract: a binding agreement formed by an offer and its acceptance.
long: The word means a knot or a tie, and Surah al-Ma'idah opens by telling believers to fulfil their contracts. Fiqh requires clear terms, a lawful subject matter, and consent free of coercion and deception. The Hanbali rule is the most generous of the four, holding any contract valid unless a text forbids it, which leaves wide room for new commercial forms, and modern Islamic finance leans on that opening.

short: A trust: anything placed in your care that you must return, or use exactly as agreed.
long: The Qur'an commands rendering trusts back to those they belong to. Legally, someone holding an amanah is not liable for loss that occurs without negligence, which is what separates a deposit from a loan or from property seized. The word is also used morally, for the trust of life, of knowledge and of public office, and its opposite is khiyanah, betrayal, which the Prophet named among the signs of hypocrisy.

short: A permanent charitable endowment: property held forever so that its income keeps serving a purpose.
long: 'Umar asked the Prophet about land he had acquired at Khaybar and was told to hold the property itself and give away its produce, which became the model. Once made, a waqf cannot be sold, given away or inherited, and it is administered for its stated beneficiaries, whether a mosque, a school, a well or a family. Historically waqf funded most of the Muslim world's hospitals, libraries and colleges, and it remains the fullest form of ongoing charity.

short: A bequest: instructions for up to a third of your estate, taking effect after death.
long: The Qur'an mentions it before the inheritance shares, and debts are settled before both. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas asked about leaving his whole estate to charity and was told a third, and that even a third is a great deal. A wasiyyah cannot be made in favour of someone who already inherits, since their share is fixed by revelation, so it is used for non heirs, for charity, and for burial and guardianship instructions.

short: Islamic inheritance: fixed shares of an estate distributed among relatives named in the Qur'an.
long: It is also called 'ilm al-fara'id, the science of the fixed portions, and it is the most mathematical corner of fiqh. The order is debts first, then any bequest up to a third, then the shares. Some heirs take a stated fraction while the remainder passes to the nearest male agnate, and because the cases interlock, one heir's presence can change another's share entirely. Most families need someone who knows the subject to work an estate out correctly.

short: Equal retaliation for murder or injury, which the victim's family may always waive for compensation.
long: The Qur'an calls it life for you, meaning that a known and strictly limited penalty restrains the endless blood feuds it replaced. It requires a court, proof and deliberate intent, and it is never a private act of revenge. The Qur'an then urges pardon and calls forgiving it an expiation for the one who forgives, and the family may accept diyah or waive everything, which classical practice treated as the better road.

short: Blood money: compensation paid to a victim's family for a killing or an injury.
long: The Qur'an prescribes it for accidental killing, alongside the freeing of a slave, and it is also what a family receives when they waive qisas for a deliberate one. The classical measure is one hundred camels, which jurists converted into gold, silver or currency, with fixed fractions for the loss of an eye, a hand or a tooth. In the classical rules the payment falls on the killer's kin group, the 'aqilah, an early form of shared insurance.

short: The small set of fixed penalties named in revelation, hedged about with very strict proof.
long: The singular is hadd, a limit; the name comes from the Qur'an's phrase the limits of God, which it uses more widely. Jurists usually count between four and seven: theft, zina, false accusation of zina, highway robbery, and for most, drinking wine and apostasy. The evidence required is deliberately near impossible, four upright eyewitnesses to the act itself in zina, and a settled maxim holds that hudud are averted by any doubt. Confessions may be withdrawn, and the classical record shows these penalties were rarely carried out.

short: Discretionary punishment, set by a judge for offences that carry no fixed penalty.
long: The word means correction. It covers the vast majority of wrongdoing, from fraud and bribery to public nuisance, and it can be a warning, a fine, imprisonment or public rebuke. The judge weighs the person, the offence and the circumstances, and most jurists hold that ta'zir must stay below the level of a hadd. This flexible category, and not the hudud, is where classical Islamic criminal justice actually did its daily work.

short: A pledge of allegiance, given to a ruler, or in Sufi orders to a spiritual guide.
long: The word comes from bay', a sale, since the one who pledges gives loyalty and receives protection in return. The Qur'an records the pledge under the tree and the pledge of the believing women, and the Prophet took bay'ah on obedience in what is good, a condition scholars stress: there is no obedience to a creature in disobedience to the Creator. In Sufi orders bay'ah to a shaykh is a commitment to a path of training, which is a different use of the same word.

short: The historic covenant under which non Muslims in a Muslim state kept their religion and protection.
long: The word means liability or covenant, and ahl al-dhimmah are the people it covered. In exchange for jizyah they were exempt from military service and from zakat, kept their own courts in matters of personal law, and had their lives, property and places of worship protected; the Prophet warned that whoever wrongs a covenanted person will find the Prophet himself his opponent on the Day of Judgement. It was a premodern arrangement of defined but unequal status, and most contemporary scholars treat it as superseded by common citizenship.

short: A tax historically paid by non Muslim men under Muslim rule, in place of military service.
long: It is named once in the Qur'an. Classical law exempted women, children, the elderly, the poor, the disabled and monks, and the rate was scaled to ability to pay. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab is reported to have granted a pension from the treasury to an elderly Jewish beggar rather than take jizyah from him. Muslims meanwhile paid zakat and were liable for military service, so the comparison was never one tax against none.

short: Zakat on wealth: normally one fortieth of qualifying savings held for a full lunar year.
long: It is distinguished from zakat al-fitr, the small fixed measure of food given per person at the end of Ramadan. It falls due on cash, gold, silver, trade stock and recoverable debts once they pass the nisab and a lunar year has turned, while crops, livestock and mined wealth have their own rates and no year requirement. Your home, personal belongings and the tools of your trade are exempt. Scholars differ over pensions, shares, and gold jewellery in regular use.

short: A scholar's answer to a specific question: advice, not a court judgement.
long: The one who gives it is a mufti and the one who asks is a mustafti. A fatwa compels nobody, it can differ from another qualified scholar's fatwa without either being wrong, and a good one depends closely on the asker's circumstances, which is why lifting someone else's fatwa off the internet can mislead you badly. A judge's ruling is the opposite: binding, and it settles the case for everyone in it.

short: A judge in an Islamic court, whose ruling binds, unlike a mufti's opinion.
long: Appointment as a qadi was treated as a heavy burden rather than an honour, and several of the great imams refused it outright. The office asks for knowledge, integrity and independence, and classical manuals warn a judge not to rule while angry, hungry or distracted. The instruction reported from the Prophet, not to decide between two people until you have heard from both, is quoted in nearly every book on the subject.

short: The higher aims of Islamic law: what its rulings exist in order to protect.
long: Al-Ghazali and later al-Shatibi set out five: religion, life, intellect, lineage and property, with dignity and sometimes freedom added by later scholars. Interests are ranked as necessities, needs and refinements, so what preserves life outweighs what merely makes life more comfortable. Maqasid explain why a ruling exists and help reasoning where the texts are silent, but most scholars insist they cannot be used to set a clear text aside.

short: Legal maxims: short principles that gather the pattern behind thousands of separate rulings.
long: Five are counted as the great ones: matters are judged by their intentions; certainty is not lifted by doubt; hardship brings ease; harm is to be removed; and custom decides. They are teaching tools and aids to reasoning rather than sources in their own right, and every one of them has recognised exceptions. Al-Suyuti's al-Ashbah wa al-Naza'ir is the best known collection.

short: Juristic preference: setting aside a strict analogy for a stronger reason of fairness or need.
long: It is chiefly a Hanafi and Maliki tool, used where the obvious qiyas would cause real hardship or would collide with a text, a consensus or plain necessity. The Hanafi allowance of manufacturing contracts, where the goods do not yet exist, is a standard example. Al-Shafi'i attacked istihsan in famous words, saying whoever practises it has made law himself, though his objection was to arbitrary preference rather than to reasoned exception.

also: certainty is not removed by doubt
short: Presumption of continuity: what was established stays in force until there is proof it changed.
long: It is why you are still in wudu when you merely doubt whether you broke it, why a missing person is presumed alive until evidence says otherwise, and why an accused person is treated as innocent until guilt is proved. It works hand in hand with the maxim that certainty is not lifted by doubt. Shafi'is and Hanbalis use it broadly, while Hanafis accept it to defend an existing state but not to establish a new right.

short: Blocking the means: forbidding something lawful because it reliably leads to something forbidden.
long: The classic proof is the Qur'anic instruction not to insult what others call upon besides God, lest they insult God in return out of ignorance. Malikis and Hanbalis use the principle heavily, while Shafi'is and Hanafis apply it more sparingly, since without limits it can be stretched to forbid nearly anything. Its mirror image, opening the means, is used to encourage whatever leads to a required good.

short: Scholarly disagreement, which classical Islam treated as normal rather than as a crisis.
long: It arises from the wording of texts, the strength of reports, differing methods, and different local customs. Scholars distinguished tolerated disagreement, where each side holds real evidence, from disagreement over what is definitively known, which is not tolerated. The Companions themselves differed and still prayed behind one another, and the standard etiquette is to act on the view you follow without condemning someone who follows another qualified one.

short: A person legally responsible: sane, and past the age of puberty.
long: The obligations of fiqh apply once both conditions are met, and the Prophet said the pen is lifted from three: the sleeper until he wakes, the child until he matures, and the one who has lost his mind until he recovers. Children are taught to pray at seven and firmly encouraged at ten, but what they do counts as voluntary and earns them reward without obligation. Puberty is judged by physical signs, or where none appear, by an age the schools commonly set around fifteen.

short: The male relative who contracts a woman's marriage on her behalf, usually her father.
long: Malikis, Shafi'is and Hanbalis hold a marriage invalid without one, citing the report that there is no marriage without a wali. Hanafis hold that an adult woman may contract her own marriage, though her guardian may object to a plainly unsuitable match. Whether a father may marry off a virgin daughter without her word is the oldest dispute here: Hanafis say no, the other three allowed it under conditions, Ibn Taymiyyah rejected it. The Prophet annulled the marriage of a woman whose father had contracted it against her will.

short: Maintenance: the husband's duty to provide housing, food and clothing for wife and children.
long: The Qur'an sets the measure by means, telling a man of wealth to spend from his wealth and one whose provision is straitened to spend from what God has given him. It is owed regardless of the wife's own income, since whatever she owns or earns remains hers alone. It continues through the waiting period after a revocable divorce, and a father's duty to maintain his children does not end when the marriage does.

short: Milk kinship: breastfeeding in infancy creates the same marriage bars that birth creates.
long: The Qur'an names milk mothers and milk sisters among those a man may not marry, and the Prophet said that nursing forbids what birth forbids. The schools differ over how much is enough: Shafi'is and Hanbalis require five separate feeds, while Hanafis and Malikis count any amount that reaches the stomach. All agree it must fall within the nursing years, which the majority place in the first two.

short: Annulment: a judge dissolving a marriage for a defect or a failure of duty.
long: Grounds recognised across the schools include serious undisclosed illness, impotence, insanity, desertion, imprisonment, failure to maintain, and harm. Malikis are the broadest here, allowing dissolution for harm in general, which is why courts in many countries follow them on this point even where another school prevails. Faskh differs from talaq because it uses up none of the husband's pronouncements, and from khul' because it requires no payment from the wife.

short: Temporary marriage for a fixed term, permitted in Twelver Shia law and prohibited in Sunni law.
long: Sunni scholars hold it was allowed early in Islam and then abolished by the Prophet, with reports placing the final prohibition at Khaybar or at the conquest of Makkah, and 'Umar's public ban is widely cited alongside them. Twelver Shia jurists hold the permission was never abrogated, and regulate mut'ah as a contract with a stated term and a stated dower. The same word has an unrelated sense in Sunni fiqh: a consolation payment made to a divorced wife.

short: Sexual intercourse outside marriage: a major sin, and one of the fixed penalty offences.
long: The Qur'an says do not go near it, calling it an immorality and an evil way, and the wording is read as forbidding the approaches to it as well as the act. The penalty carries a bar of proof so high it is almost never reached, four upright witnesses to the act itself, and the same passage punishes those who make the accusation without them. Islamic law discourages prying, and consistently prefers concealment and repentance to exposure.

short: Apostasy: abandoning Islam after having accepted it.
long: Classical law treated open apostasy as a capital offence, drawing on prophetic reports rather than on the Qur'an, which mentions apostasy several times without prescribing any worldly penalty and states plainly that there is no compulsion in religion. Hanafis did not apply the death penalty to a woman who apostatised, and jurists across the schools required that repentance be invited first. Many contemporary scholars read the classical rulings as addressing public treason within a specific political order rather than private belief, and the question is actively debated.

short: Sale: the exchange of property for property by mutual consent.
long: The Qur'an states that God has permitted trade and forbidden riba, and the Prophet himself worked as a merchant before prophethood. A valid sale needs a known price, a known item the seller can actually deliver, ownership or authority to sell it, and consent untouched by deception. Fiqh names many specific forms, among them salam, paid now and delivered later, and murabahah, sold at a disclosed markup.

short: Hire or lease: paying for the use of something, or for another person's labour.
long: The Qur'an mentions hiring a worker in the story of Musa in Madyan and instructs that a nursing mother be paid her due. The contract needs a defined benefit, a defined period and a known wage agreed in advance. The reported instruction to give the worker his wage before his sweat dries is the most quoted line in the whole chapter. In Islamic finance, ijarah is the leasing structure used in place of an interest bearing loan.

short: A sale at a disclosed cost plus markup, widely used in Islamic banking in place of lending.
long: In its classical form the seller states what the goods cost him and what profit he is adding, so the buyer knows both figures. Modern banks use it to finance purchases: the bank buys the asset, then sells it on to the customer at a higher price payable in instalments. Supporters point out that the bank takes real ownership and real risk in between; critics answer that the outcome tracks interest too closely, and the disagreement among scholars is genuine and unsettled.

short: A partnership where one side provides capital and the other the work, sharing agreed profits.
long: Losses of money fall on the investor while the working partner loses his effort, unless he was negligent or broke the terms. Profit must be divided by a stated ratio and never as a fixed sum, since a guaranteed return would quietly turn the arrangement into an interest bearing loan. Musharakah is its sibling, in which both sides put in capital and share profit and loss by agreement. Both predate Islam and were confirmed rather than invented by it, and both underpin profit sharing accounts today.

short: Cooperative insurance, built on mutual donation, offered as an alternative to conventional policies.
long: Participants contribute to a shared fund on the basis of tabarru', donation, and the fund pays claims, while an operator manages it for a fee or an agreed share. It was designed to answer the objections scholars raise against conventional insurance, namely gharar, resemblance to gambling, and interest bearing reserves. Not every scholar accepts that the difference is substantive, and some hold conventional insurance permissible under necessity where no alternative is available.

short: Meat from an animal slaughtered in the Islamic way, with the name of God pronounced over it.
long: The throat is cut swiftly with a sharp blade, severing the windpipe and the blood vessels, and the animal must be alive and treated gently beforehand; the Prophet ordered the blade to be sharpened, the animal spared distress, and the knife kept out of its sight. The Qur'an also permits the food of the People of the Book, and scholars differ over whether ordinary commercial meat in Jewish and Christian countries falls under that permission. Pork, blood, carrion and anything dedicated to other than God remain forbidden either way.

short: Intoxicants. Wine and anything else that clouds the mind, forbidden in the Qur'an.
long: The prohibition arrived in stages, ending with the command to shun it as a defilement from the work of Satan. The Prophet's rule that whatever intoxicates in large amounts is forbidden in small amounts extends the ban to every intoxicant, and it is the textbook example of qiyas at work. Hanafis kept the word khamr technically for grape wine while forbidding other intoxicants under a separate heading, arriving at the same practical result. Scholars differ over intoxicating substances used as medicine where no alternative exists.
